raw_case_text:
The first patient, a 28-year-old man native to Gabon was living in the Noya region (Figure 1). This patient was received and examined in April 2019. He was characterized by a severe and violent headache with a fever of 39 C. He took paracetamol for symptoms relief, but no improvement was noted. HBV, HCV, HIV, syphilis, and malaria testing were all negative. The diagnosis of HAT was done by microscopic analysis and revealed the presence of trypanosomes in aspiration fluid of the ganglion (Figure 2). Later on, the diagnosis of phase 2 HAT was confirmed based on the presence of trypanosomes in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed clear liquid and pleocytosis at 27/mm3. He was admitted at the intensive care unit due to altered state of consciousness. The clinical examinations on admission revealed cachexia; multiple dermabrasion on the abdomen related to scratching lesions; impaired consciousness with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9/15 and a meningeal syndrome, and motor deficit. The biological assessment revealed severe anemia with a hemoglobin level of 8.7 g/dL, an important inflammatory syndrome with a C-reactive protein (CRP) at 243 mg/L and leukocytes: 15,700/mm3. The brain computed tomographic (CT) scan showed a meningoencephalitis aspect with multiple capsulo-lenticulo-insular hypodensities. The patient received a specific combination treatment of eflornithine and nifurtimox (NECT) for the HAT as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for second-stage T. b. gambiense infection for all endemic countries. During th course of intensive care treatment, the patient died of complications, eschars stage 4 wound, and malnutrition.
The second patient, a 41-year-old man, originally from Indonesia, living in Gabon for the past 8 years, in the Kango town in the Komo department (Figure 1) working in the Gabonese forest for the Olam company. He was admitted in July 2019 to the Hospital for altered state of consciousness. Upon his arrival at the hospital, the clinical picture was marked by intermittent fever (peak of temperature at 39.7 C) associated with chills, headaches, polyarthralgia, sleeping disorders and we found also this patient with acute mastoiditis. After a microscopic analysis which was negative, an analysis of the CSF revealed the presence of trypanosomes by the card agglutination test for trypanosomiasis (CATT+) (+1/16) and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid reveals clear crystalline fluid, glycorrhachia at 2.76 mmol/L with a capillary blood glucose of 4.78 mmol/L, CSF protein level of 1.7 mmol/L, and a leucocytes count of 9,000/mm3. The presence of trypanosoma parasites in CSF suggests second-stage HAT. The blood count showed neutrophils (2,070/mm3), hemoglobin (10 g/dL), and a CRP at 123 mg/L. As with the first patient, several clinical examinations were done (HBV, HCV, HIV, syphilis, malaria test), but all were negative. However, cytobacteriological urine examination revealed the presence of Enterobacter aerogenes. The patient was treated with ceftriaxone antibiotic for its bacterial infection. Regarding the treatment of HAT, the patient received NECT as per WHO recommendations. The neurological evolution was favorable, marked by a normal consciousness after treatment. The patient return to his country safely.
To confirm the diagnosis of HAT, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed to characterize the Trypanosoma species. The sequences obtained (around 1,200 nucleotides) have been deposited in Genbank under the accession numbers MT460094-MT460095. We used maximum likelihood (ML) as described previously, to examine the relationship of both sequences obtained with the different trypanosome species known. The tree was built (Figure 3) using MEGA software.

subjective.chief_complaint: Two adult male patients in Gabon presented with second-stage neurological symptoms: a 28-year-old Gabonese man with severe headache, high fever (39 C), and altered consciousness, and a 41-year-old Indonesian forestry worker with intermittent high fever (39.7 C), chills, headaches, polyarthralgia, sleep disturbances, and altered consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Patient 1 (28-year-old male from Noya region, Gabon, April 2019) developed violent headache and paracetamol-refractory fever (39 C) progressing to coma (GCS 9/15). Patient 2 (41-year-old Indonesian man working in the Kango forest, Gabon, for 8 years, July 2019) developed intermittent fevers up to 39.7 C, chills, headaches, polyarthralgia, sleep-wake disorder, acute mastoiditis, and altered sensorium.
subjective.past_medical_history: Patient 1 was a native of Noya, Gabon; Patient 2 was an Indonesian expatriate forestry worker in Komo department, Gabon, for 8 years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, severe headache, altered consciousness, cachexia/pruritic excoriations (Patient 1), and chills, polyarthralgia, sleep disorder, and mastoiditis (Patient 2).

objective.physical_examination: Patient 1: temperature 39 C, cachexia, abdominal scratching dermabrasions, GCS 9/15, meningeal signs, motor deficit, and later stage 4 pressure eschars. Patient 2: intermittent fever peaking at 39.7 C, altered consciousness, and acute mastoiditis.
objective.routine_investigations: Patient 1: severe anemia (Hb 8.7 g/dL), CRP 243 mg/L, WBC 15,700/mm3. Patient 2: Hb 10 g/dL, neutrophils 2,070/mm3, CRP 123 mg/L, positive CATT (+1/16), and urine culture positive for Enterobacter aerogenes. Both patients tested negative for HBV, HCV, HIV, and syphilis.
objective.advanced_workup: Patient 1: lymph node aspirate and CSF (clear, 27 WBC/mm3) showed live trypanosomes; brain CT showed meningoencephalitis with multiple capsulo-lenticulo-insular hypodensities. Patient 2: CSF (clear, 9,000 WBC/mm3, glucose 2.76 mmol/L vs capillary 4.78 mmol/L, protein 1.7 mmol/L) revealed trypanosomes; PCR and ~1,200 bp sequencing (GenBank MT460094-MT460095) confirmed Trypanosoma brucei gambiense.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Second-stage meningoencephalitic Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT) caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense in two patients. Malaria was excluded in both patients by negative malaria testing. Both patients were treated with WHO-recommended nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy (NECT) (plus ceftriaxone for Enterobacter aerogenes UTI in Patient 2); Patient 1 died in the ICU from malnutrition and stage 4 decubitus complications, whereas Patient 2 recovered normal consciousness and returned safely to Indonesia.
